meta.location: The city of Gid, and the borders by the east sea
principles: A refusal made on principle and on arithmetic
A city taken without a death
Restraint exercised at the moment of advantage

world_behind.title: Moroni refuses the exchange he negotiated
world_behind.text: Verse 2 has him decline unless Ammoron withdraws, because he will not grant him any more power than he already has.

world_behind.title: The anger has a specific cause
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has Moroni angrier because the other man knew perfectly well that his cause was fraudulent. Alma 54:16 to 24 preserves his letter, in which he claims his fathers were wronged of the government; this verse is Moroni's judgment on a document the reader has just read.

world_behind.title: He searches his own ranks for a Lamanite
world_behind.text: Verse 4 has him search his own ranks for a descendant of Laman, and verse 5 finds a man named Laman who had been a servant of the king Amalickiah murdered. Alma 47:22 to 29 records that murder and the servants who fled; one of them has been in the Nephite army ever since.

world_behind.title: The man was one of the murdered king's servants
world_behind.text: Verse 5 identifies him as a servant of the king Amalickiah killed, which makes him one of the men falsely accused in Alma 47.

world_behind.title: The wine was prepared strong on purpose
world_behind.text: Verse 13 says the wine was strong, having been prepared in its strength. Alma 55:31 and 32 has the Nephites afterwards testing every liquor on a prisoner before drinking, which is the countermeasure this episode taught them.

world_behind.title: The prisoners are armed inside the walls
world_behind.text: Verses 16 and 17 arm the prisoners inside the wall, women and children included, in profound silence. Alma 54:3 had reported that the Lamanites held Nephite women and children while Moroni held none; that asymmetry is what put them behind that wall.

world_behind.title: Moroni declines to kill the drunk
world_behind.text: Verses 18 and 19 say the Nephites could have slaughtered them and that he would not, because it would have brought injustice on him.

words.text: To plead, to petition formally. The phrase sue for peace occurs once in scripture. Moroni uses it of what he means to force on the Lamanites by seeking death among them until they ask.
Called out to, challenged. The word appears once in all of scripture. The guards hail Laman as he approaches, and his answer is the whole deception in three sentences.

An allotted issue of food or drink. The word occurs a single time in scripture. The guards reason that they will get more wine issued later, which is the argument that persuades them to drink what they have.
Treated at 2 Nephi 27:4, in Isaiah's figure for a people who stagger without wine. Here it is literal, four times in five verses, and it is the mechanism of the whole operation.
Absence of sound. The phrase profound silence turns up just once in scripture. Mormon uses it of arming an entire prisoner population, women and children included, without waking the guards.
Wrong done. Mormon uses the word for what Moroni would have brought on himself by killing sleeping drunk men. It is the record's own explanation of the restraint.

phrases.term: He knew that Ammoron had a perfect knowledge of his fraud
phrases.text: Mormon explains the anger. Alma 54 printed Ammoron's justification; this verse says Moroni believed the man knew it was false when he wrote it.

phrases.term: I will not grant unto him that he shall have any more power than what he hath got
phrases.text: The refusal stated as policy. An exchange would return Lamanite soldiers, so Moroni declines it on the same arithmetic that made his terms hard in Alma 54.

phrases.term: I will seek death among them until they shall sue for peace
phrases.text: The alternative to the exchange, said plainly. What follows is a plan that takes a city and kills nobody, which sits oddly beside this sentence and is left to sit.

phrases.term: Perhaps he might find a man who was a descendant of Laman among them
phrases.text: The search that makes the plan possible. Mormon notes the Nephite army contained such men, and that finding one took looking.

phrases.term: He was one of the servants of the king who was murdered by Amalickiah
phrases.text: Laman's history in one clause. Alma 47 had these servants blamed for the killing and hunted; one of them now walks back into a Lamanite camp with wine.

phrases.term: Fear not; behold, I am a Lamanite
phrases.text: Every word of it true. The deception is built out of accurate statements, and Mormon lets the reader notice.

phrases.term: Let us keep of our wine till we go against the Nephites to battle
phrases.text: Laman argues against the drinking, and verse 10 says the saying only made them more desirous. The refusal is the persuasion.

phrases.term: It was strong, having been prepared in its strength
phrases.text: Mormon supplies the one fact that explains the outcome. The wine was made for this, and he says so only when the guards have drunk it.

phrases.term: All those things were done in a profound silence
phrases.text: An entire prison population armed without a sound. The sentence is the climax of the operation, and it contains no violence.

phrases.term: He did not delight in murder or bloodshed, but he delighted in the saving of his people
phrases.text: Mormon repeats the judgment of Alma 48 at the moment it costs something. The Nephites could have killed everyone and did not.
The morning picture. Surrounded outside and outnumbered inside, the Lamanites judge a fight pointless and give up their weapons.

verses.label: v. 8–13
verses.title: A refusal that works better than an offer
verses.text: The deception is preserved as dialogue and the turn in it is a denial. The guards ask for the wine; the answer is "Let us keep of our wine till we go against the Nephites to battle." The record then explains the effect at once: "this saying only made them more desirous to drink of the wine." Their own reasoning is quoted back as well, "We are weary, therefore let us take of the wine, and by and by we shall receive wine for our rations." The trick is not persuasion but withholding, and the record says so rather than leaving it to be inferred.

verses.label: v. 17
verses.title: The arming described by category, not by number
verses.text: The record specifies exactly who received weapons and draws the line by capacity: "Yea, even to their women, and all those of their children, as many as were able to use a weapon of war, when Moroni had armed all those prisoners of the Nephites." No count is given. The clause as many as were able does the work a number would, and it makes the prisoners in the city into a force without stating how large it was.

verses.label: v. 18–19
verses.title: The massacre that did not happen, reported anyway
verses.text: The record states an option that was available and declined: "had they awakened the Lamanites, behold they were drunken and the Nephites could have slain them." Verse 19 gives the reason for not doing it, and it is a claim about a man's character rather than about tactics: "this was not the desire of Moroni; he did not delight in murder or bloodshed, but he delighted in the saving of his people from destruction." A war record pauses to describe a killing that was never carried out.

verses.label: v. 22–24
verses.title: A city changes hands with no fighting reported
verses.text: The result is given as a morning discovery: "this was done in the night-time, so that when the Lamanites awoke in the morning they beheld that they were surrounded by the Nephites, and their prisoners were armed." The surrender is then reported as a calculation rather than a defeat: "they saw that the Nephites had power over them; and in these circumstances they found that it was not expedient that they should fight with the Nephites." No casualties are named on either side.

verses.label: v. 25
verses.title: The same use for prisoners as two chapters earlier
verses.text: The record puts the new captives to the identical task the last set were given: "he did cause the Lamanites, whom he had taken prisoners, that they should commence a labor in strengthening the fortifications round about the city Gid." Alma 53:4–5 reports the same arrangement, prisoners building the works that hold them, in the same city. The repetition is not remarked on, and the second instance is described in almost the same words as the first.

verses.label: v. 30–32
verses.title: A counter-tactic, and the reasoning that defeats it
verses.text: The record reports the enemy adopting the trick: "many times did they attempt to administer of their wine to the Nephites, that they might destroy them with poison or with drunkenness." The defence given is not vigilance but an argument, stated as a piece of ordinary reasoning: "they were thus cautious that no poison should be administered among them; for if their wine would poison a Lamanite it would also poison a Nephite." A test anyone could apply is written into the account, and it is the symmetry of the substance that supplies it.

chapter.title: A city is taken and nobody is killed
chapter.text: The chapter opens with Moroni promising to seek death among them and ends with a surrender and a liberation. Mormon reports both without reconciling them.

chapter.title: The refusal is arithmetic before it is principle
chapter.text: An exchange returns fighting men to the enemy. Moroni gives that reason in verse 2, and the moral argument in verse 1 sits beside it.

chapter.title: The deception is made of true statements
chapter.text: Verse 5 establishes that the claim is true: the man found is "one whose name was Laman; and he was one of the servants of the king who was murdered by Amalickiah." What he says at verse 8 is therefore accurate, "Fear not; behold, I am a Lamanite," as is the second half, "we have escaped from the Nephites." The wine is real and the escape is real. The record supplies the man's credentials before the speech, so the reader can check every sentence of the deception against the facts already given.

chapter.title: Reluctance is the persuasion
chapter.text: Verse 10 has him argue against drinking, "Let us keep of our wine till we go against the Nephites to battle," and the record states the effect in the same verse, "this saying only made them more desirous to drink of the wine." Verse 11 gives the guards their own reasoning, "we are weary... by and by we shall receive wine for our rations." Verse 12 is his consent in seven words, "You may do according to your desires." The plan works because the guards overrule him, and the record supplies their argument as well as his.

chapter.title: The decisive detail is withheld until it acts
chapter.text: The wine was prepared strong. Mormon gives it in verse 13, after the drinking has started, which is how a reader would have learned it.

chapter.title: Women and children are armed
chapter.text: Verse 17 includes them among those able to use a weapon. Moroni had threatened this in Alma 54 and here does it inside a prison.

chapter.title: Restraint is given a reason
chapter.text: Not mercy alone, but that killing the drunk would bring injustice on him. Mormon states the principle at the moment of maximum advantage.

chapter.title: The freed prisoners become an army
chapter.text: Verse 24 has them join Moroni and add great strength. The operation solves the manpower problem the exchange was meant to solve.

applications.title: Assume some opponents already know
applications.text: Moroni's anger rose because he knew that Ammoron had a perfect knowledge of his own fraud. Not everyone opposing you is working from bad information, and treating a knowing opponent as a confused one spends effort you need elsewhere.

applications.title: Check what a deal gives the other side
applications.text: Moroni refused an exchange that would have returned soldiers to his enemy. Before accepting an arrangement, work out what it restores to the party you are contending with.

applications.title: Look through your own ranks first
applications.text: The plan required a Lamanite and Moroni had one. When you need an unusual capability, search what you already have before looking outside.

applications.title: Notice when resistance is doing the persuading
applications.text: Laman's argument against drinking made them want it more. Be alert to reluctance that functions as encouragement, in yourself and in others.

applications.title: Match the volume of the work to what it can survive
applications.text: The arming of the prisoners, women and children included, was carried out in a profound silence. Some tasks fail the moment they are noticed, and announcing one of those is a forfeit dressed up as courage.

applications.title: Do not take the advantage that would cost you your case
applications.text: Moroni could have killed sleeping men and would not. When you have an opening that would compromise the ground you are standing on, leave it.

applications.title: Give the rescued a place to work
applications.text: The freed Nephite prisoners joined Moroni's army and became a great strength to it. People you helped out of a bad position are often the most committed help available, so make room for them instead of filing them away as beneficiaries.

applications.title: Do not accept what you cannot check
applications.text: The Nephites would not partake of Lamanite wine until it had been tried first. When an offer comes from someone who has already attempted to harm you, the useful question is whether you have any way to confirm it, and looking fine is not confirmation.

questions.text: What makes me angrier, being wronged or knowing they knew better?
What am I about to agree to that would strengthen the thing I oppose?
Who has been falsely blamed and is still standing nearby?
Have I ever deceived someone using only true statements?
What in my life was prepared in its strength before I tasted it?
What have I done well that required doing quietly?
What advantage have I declined, and did I say why?

anchor.quote: I will not exchange prisoners with Ammoron

entries.reason: the terms Moroni offered before the reply arrived

targets.quote: I will not exchange prisoners, save it be on conditions
targets.verse_text: But behold, it supposeth me that I talk to you concerning these things in vain; or it supposeth me that thou art a child of hell; therefore I will close my epistle by telling you that I will not exchange prisoners, save it be on conditions that ye will deliver up a man and his wife and his children, for one prisoner; if this be the case that ye will do it, I will exchange.
